procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (implied, as a first information report was lodged and accused were remanded to police custody by a Magistrate)
procedural_history.impugned_order: The High Court held all the three respondents guilty of contempt of court and convicted them accordingly. The High Court imposed a sentence of fine of Rs. 200/- on the first respondent and of administering an admonition to respondents 2 and 3. The High Court discharged respondents two and three after due admonition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A first information report was lodged on Sept. 11, 1967 regarding the loss of life of a person when two groups of people clashed. On Sept, 20, 1967 the first appellant made a statement charging one of the groups being guilty of deliberate conspiracy to commit the murder and alleging that a prominent member of that party had given instructions for this. The respondent along with his two brothers was arrested on Sept . .23, 1967 and on the next day the Magistrate remanded the accused to police custody. In its issue dated Sept. 23. 1967 a newspaper of which the second appellant was the editor printed the statement of the first appellant. Later on all the three accused were produced before the Magistrate. The respondent filed a petition under ss. 3 and ·4 of the Contempt of Court's Act, l 952 against the first appellant, second appellant and the printer of the newspapers. The High Court found all the persons guilty of contempt of court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants A. K. Gopalan and P. Govinda Pillai secured a certificate of fitness under Art. 134(1)(c). The Supreme Court allowed the appeal of A. K. Gopalan and dismissed the appeal of P. Govinda Pillai. The conviction against P. Govinda Pillai was maintained.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal of A. K. Gopalan is allowed and the appeal of P. Govinda Pillai is dismissed.
decision.conviction_status: In the result we maintain the conviction entered by the High Court against the appellant P. Govinda Pillai.
directions: The fine, if already paid by A. K. Gopalan, shall be refunded.

issue.issue_text: Whether the first appellant, A. K. Gopalan, was guilty of contempt of court for making a statement when there was no evidence that any proceedings in a court were imminent on that date.

facts: A fatal incident occurred on September 11, 1967, and a First Information Report was lodged the same day.
The first appellant, A. K. Gopalan, made a statement regarding the incident on September 20, 1967.
An arrest in the case was made on September 23, 1967.
Gopalan's statement was published in a newspaper on September 25, 1967.
law: Contempt of court can be committed by making a statement that is likely to prejudice the due course of justice in proceedings that are "imminent," even if they have not actually begun.
application: The Court determined that the crucial date for judging A. K. Gopalan's actions was the date he made the statement, September 20, 1967, not the later date of its publication.
The majority opinion found that there was no evidence presented to prove that any court proceedings were imminent on September 20, 1967.
The Court distinguished Gopalan's case from that of the newspaper editor, for whom the relevant date was September 25, by which time an arrest had been made, making proceedings imminent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court (by majority) decided that A. K. Gopalan was not guilty of contempt of court because there was no evidence that court proceedings were imminent on the specific date he made his statement.

issue.issue_text: Whether the second appellant, P. Govinda Pillai, was guilty of contempt of court for publishing a statement at a time when proceedings in a court were imminent, given that the accused had already been arrested.

facts: The accused, K. P. Noordeen, was arrested on September 23, 1967, in connection with a serious cognizable case.
On September 24, a Magistrate remanded the accused to police custody.
On September 25, 1967, a statement about the case was published in the "Deshabhimani" newspaper, of which P. Govinda Pillai was the editor.
law: Publishing a statement that is calculated to prejudice a party or interfere with the due course of justice constitutes contempt of court.
This rule applies not only when proceedings are pending but also when they are "imminent."
application: The Court determined that the key question was whether proceedings were imminent on September 25, the date of publication.
It reasoned that the arrest of the accused in a serious case, followed by their production before a magistrate for remand, was a clear indicator that legal proceedings were imminent.
The Court stated that an arrest signifies that the police are "prima facie on the right track."

It rejected the idea that imminence only begins when the police file a final report (charge sheet), arguing that such a rule would cause harm by encouraging public investigation and discussion while a case is under police investigation.
The possibility that the police might later find the accused innocent was deemed irrelevant to whether the proceedings were imminent at the time of publication.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the accused had already been arrested and remanded by a magistrate, court proceedings were imminent at the time P. Govinda Pillai published the statement. Therefore, he was found guilty of contempt of court, and his conviction was upheld.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the first appellant, A. K. Gopalan, was guilty of contempt of court for making a statement when there was no evidence that any proceedings in a court were imminent on that date.
appellant_arguments: The relevant date to consider is September 20, when the statement was made, not the later date of publication.
On September 20, there were no proceedings pending in a court.
There was no evidence that any court proceedings were imminent on the date the statement was made.
The lodging of a first information report does not by itself establish that proceedings in a court were imminent.
There is no evidence that the first appellant was instrumental in getting the statement published on a later date.
respondent_arguments: The crucial date is not September 20, when the statement was made, but September 25, when the newspaper published it.
Even on September 20, criminal proceedings were imminent, and the appellant had no reasonable cause to believe they were not.
The circumstances of the case, including a murder, an ongoing police investigation, and the seizure of weapons, made it clear that proceedings were imminent.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the second appellant, P. Govinda Pillai, was guilty of contempt of court for publishing a statement at a time when proceedings in a court were imminent, given that the accused had already been arrested.
appellant_arguments: The provided text does not detail the specific arguments made by the second appellant.
respondent_arguments: The publication of the statement occurred after the accused had been arrested on September 23.
The arrest of the accused demonstrates that judicial proceedings were imminent at the time of publication.

cases.principle: The jurisdiction to punish for contempt of court is not confined to cases in which a cause is actually pending in the High Court at the moment of publication, but is also attracted if proceedings are imminent.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for contempt of court based on a publication cannot be sustained if, at the time of the publication, there is no evidence that any judicial proceedings were pending or imminent.
obiter: It is common knowledge that a murder in broad day light when two groups of people clash is sure to be investigated into and made the subject of criminal proceedings.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's finding hinges on the distinction between making a statement before judicial proceedings are imminent and publishing it after they have become so. The first appellant, A. K. Gopalan, was found not guilty because when he made his statement, there was no evidence that court proceedings were imminent, as no arrest had been made. Conversely, the second appellant, P. Govinda Pillai, was found guilty because he published the statement after the accused had been arrested, at which point proceedings were considered imminent, and the publication had a tendency to prejudice the trial.
legal_tests_applied: The essence of the offence of contempt is conduct calculated to produce an atmosphere of prejudice in which proceedings will have to go on, or a tendency to interfere with the due course of justice.

To constitute contempt, it is not necessary to show that a judge or jury will in fact be prejudiced; the test is whether the publication has a tendency to or is calculated to prejudice the parties or interfere with the due course of justice.
The jurisdiction to punish for contempt is attracted when judicial proceedings are pending or imminent.
A person is guilty of contempt if, 'knowing or having good reason to believe that criminal proceedings are imminent, he chooses to publish matters calculate~ to prejudice a fair trial.'
why_appellant_lost: The second appellant, P. Govinda Pillai, lost his appeal because he published the prejudicial statement at a time when judicial proceedings were imminent.
The imminence of the proceedings was established by the fact that the accused had already been arrested on September 23, prior to the publication on September 25.

Publishing a statement calculated to prejudice a fair trial after an arrest has been made constitutes contempt of court, as the publisher has good reason to believe that criminal proceedings are imminent.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded against the second appellant because the act of publication occurred after the accused had been arrested, which is the point at which judicial proceedings are considered imminent.
The publication of a statement that tends to 'prejudice mankind against the accused' when a trial is imminent is an interference with the due course of justice and constitutes contempt.
The court affirmed that the arrest of the accused was the critical event that made the subsequent publication an act of contempt, as it was then clear that a judicial proceeding would follow.
policy_considerations: The power to punish for contempt must be exercised with 'circumspection, carefully and with restraint and only in cases where it is necessary for maintaining the course of justice pure and unaffected.'

The law of contempt must balance the liberty of free speech and the duty of a free press to comment on matters of public interest with the fundamental right of a citizen to have a fair trial in an atmosphere free of prejudice.
It would be an 'undue restriction on the liherty of free speech to lay down that even before any arrest has been made there should be no comments on the facts of a particular case.'

The purpose of contempt law is to prevent publications that tend to 'reduce the Court which has to try the case to impotence, so far as the effectual elimination of prejudice and preposse.'~ion is concerned.'
